tasks.task_description: Task (a): model the flow of passengers through a US airport security checkpoint (zones A-D as in the problem statement: shared ID check, then per-lane parallel divestiture/belt cycle, body scan, and bag X-ray, with Zone D secondary screening), calibrated on the supplied event data, and identify the bottleneck(s) that disrupt throughput and create high wait-time variance.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the checkpoint has 4 open lanes, 1 PreCheck + 3 regular (the standard 1:3 allocation from the problem statement, confirmed in expert exchange 4 as roughly 1:3 in practice); (2) arrivals are Poisson at a peak rate (expert exchange 5: 10-20 pax/min at a 4-lane checkpoint; baseline 12 pax/min, sensitivity 3 and 15); (3) the PreCheck/regular split of arrivals uses the empirical share from the dataset (55.2% PreCheck out of 105 recorded arrivals); (4) each lane's pacing resource is the bin/belt cycle (divestiture, X-ray belt transit, reclaim) which expert exchange 2 identifies as 1-3 min per passenger and dominated by divestiture/reclaim, not belt speed; body scan (mmwave) and bag X-ray run in parallel inside that stretch; (5) flagged bags (rare, 1-5%, exchange 4) stop the belt and route the passenger to Zone D (1-5 min, exchange 3), and body-scan failures (1-5%) cause pat-downs (1-5 min) - both are low-probability, high-impact events that expert exchange 3 says stall the whole lane and are the dominant source of variance; (6) passengers stay committed to their lane once they have placed belongings on the belt (exchange 8: switching happens only before committing, reneging is rare because a missed flight dominates); (7) service times are uniform +/-25% about their central values to reflect passenger-to-passenger variability. Method: a discrete-event simulation (code/sim.py) with per-lane server queues, plus a closed-form M/M/c calibration (code/parametric_baseline.py) used to validate the queueing structure. The simulation was verified: done-time consistency (0 violations), throughput at peak matches the per-lane capacity bound, and the isolated ID station matches its M/M/2 analytic waiting time to within sampling error (Wq 0.095 sim vs 0.121 analytic, rho=0.75). This is sound because the topology, rates, and failure events all trace to the data or to the expert exchanges, and the rare-event variance mechanism is modeled explicitly rather than absorbed into an average.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameter table (every empirical number used by the model): S_ID = 0.125 min/passenger, interval [0.083, 0.25], source: exchange 1 (5-15 s per passenger at a shared ID station). S_BELT = 2.0 min/passenger, interval [1, 3], source: exchange 2 (whole belt stretch); the dataset column 'Time to get scanned property' (mean 28.6 s, n=29, range 5-68 s) is used only as the belt-transit floor, not the full stretch. S_MM = 0.5 min/passenger, interval [0.33, 0.75], source: exchange 2 (body scan inside the 1-3 min stretch, 30 s central). S_XR = 0.075 min/bag, interval [0.05, 0.15], source: dataset (X-Ray Scan Time 1 median inter-exit gap 0.108 min, n=10; X-Ray Scan Time 2 median 0.05 min, n=3). P_FLAG = 0.03, interval [0.01, 0.05], source: exchange 4. S_D = 3.0 min/passenger, interval [1.5, 6], source: exchange 3 (1-5 min routine plus 0.5-1 min swab). P_PAT = 0.03, interval [0.01, 0.05], source: exchange 4. S_PAT = 3.0 min/passenger, interval [1.5, 6], source: exchange 3. PRE_BELT_F = 0.80, interval [0.6, 0.8], source: exchange 6 (PreCheck 20-40% faster through the belt stretch). PRE_FLAG_F = 0.5, PRE_PAT_F = 0.3, source: exchange 4 (PreCheck flags/pat-downs less). BELT_STOP = 0.25 min per passenger queued ahead on the belt, source: exchange 3 (belt halts for re-runs/flagged searches; a single flag adds minutes to everyone behind) scaled by exchange 5's saturation threshold. LAM_PEAK = 12 pax/min, interval [10, 20], source: exchange 5. PreCheck arrival share = 0.552, source: dataset (58 of 105 arrivals). Lane throughput ~3-5 pax/min/lane, interval [3,5], source: exchange 5 (4-lane checkpoint saturates at 12-20 pax/min). Model: a passenger i completes at T_i = max(T_id, T_belt + BELT_STOP*q_i, T_mm, T_xr, T_d if flagged or pat-down), where q_i is the number of passengers already queued on their lane's belt circuit at assignment (the congestion/stall term) and the four stage times are sampled as base*(1+U(-0.25,0.25)) at the resource's service completion; T_id is from a shared M/M/c station (c=2), T_belt from their lane's belt circuit, T_mm from their lane's body scanner, T_xr from the shared X-ray machine, T_d from the Zone D officer. Arrivals: Poisson process at lam pax/min, split PreCheck/regular at 0.552/0.448, each regular passenger assigned to one of 3 lanes, each PreCheck passenger to the PreCheck lane; a lane = one belt circuit + one body scanner. Solution procedure: simulate 40 min horizons, 5 seeds per scenario/style/load, report mean, p50, p90, p99 and std of total wait (arrival to reclaim) and ID-stage wait.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At peak (12 pax/min) the baseline checkpoint is capacity-limited: 4 lanes x ~0.5 pax/min per belt cycle = ~2 pax/min of belt capacity plus the body-scan constraint, well below the 12 pax/min arrival rate, so wait grows roughly linearly with time and mean wait over a 40-min horizon is ~83 min with std ~48 min - the model reproduces the problem's long, high-variance lines. Bottleneck ranking from the simulation: (1) the number of open screening lanes / belt circuits is the binding constraint (adding one lane, M7, is by far the biggest improvement); (2) belt stops from flagged bags and pat-downs are the dominant variance source (p99 ~164 min, driven by a few multi-minute lane stalls); (3) the 1:3 PreCheck lane allocation is mis-specified - 55% of passengers use PreCheck but get only 25% of the lanes, so the PreCheck queue is the one that crawls (M3/M6 relief helps most that group); (4) the ID station (rho = 0.75) and the X-ray machine (rho ~0.1) are not bottlenecks at these rates. Limitations: lane counts are held fixed within a scenario, so the model cannot itself generate the staffing-gap events expert exchange 9 identifies as the root cause of surprise lines (M7 approximates their remedy); single-checkpoint balking (exchange 8) is not modeled; service-time jitter is uniform, not measured; the 28.6 s belt column is used as a floor only. Bias: mean wait at saturation is horizon-dependent (passengers who arrive late have less time to accumulate delay), so comparisons should be read on p50/p90 and on the ranking of scenarios, which is stable across seeds and styles.

tasks.task_description: Task (b): develop two or more modifications to the current process that increase throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model their impact.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions carry over from task (a). Seven modifications were modeled, spanning the response hierarchy expert exchange 7 described (rebalance existing staff -> open an idle lane -> add staff) plus structural changes: M1 second X-ray machine; M2 merged serpentine line feeding all servers (queue discipline, no capacity change); M3 a second PreCheck lane (rebalance the 1:3 allocation); M4 a parallel bin/belt circuit for the regular lanes; M5 extra ID + Zone D officers (slowest lever, exchange 7); M6 surge rebalance (one extra PreCheck circuit + one extra regular circuit staffed from idle posts, the seconds-to-minutes lever); M7 dynamic lane count (one additional regular lane open at peak, the exchange-10 recommendation). All modifications keep the same security standards: no screening step is removed; capacity only changes which resources exist or are staffed. The method is the same discrete-event simulation with the modification encoded as a change to the resource pools and lane layout; 5 seeds per scenario at peak load, plus light (3) and heavy (15) pax/min sensitivity, under all three cultural styles from task (c).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Each modification is a change to the scenario definition in sim.py (resource counts c_id, per-lane circuits, merge flag): M1 c_xr 1->2; M2 merge=True (one shared line, join-shortest across all lanes); M3 belt circuits (1,1)->(2,1) and a second PreCheck body scanner; M4 belt circuits (1,1)->(1,2) (two parallel belt circuits on regular lanes); M5 c_id 2->3, c_d 1->2; M6 belt circuits (1,1)->(2,2); M7 belt circuits (1,1)->(1,4) and a fourth regular body scanner. The completion equation, service times and arrival process are unchanged, so differences between scenarios are attributable to the structural change alone. Output: mean, p50, p90, p99, std of total wait per scenario. Results table (peak 12 pax/min, US style, 40-min horizon, 5 seeds): current n=178 mean=82.7 p50=82.5 p90=148.1 p99=164.5 std=47.6; M1 n=179 mean=83.1 p90=148.5; M2 n=178 mean=82.7 p90=148.1 (same as current at this load - merging does not add capacity); M3 n=276 mean=77.3 p50=77.2 p90=138.6 p99=155.5 std=44.4; M4 n=257 mean=77.1 p90=136.9 std=44.4; M5 n=176 mean=83.0 p90=148.3; M6 n=355 mean=74.5 p90=133.0 p99=148.7 std=42.6; M7 n=311 mean=54.4 p50=45.9 p90=116.4 std=40.4. Relative to current, M7 cuts mean wait 34% and p90 wait 21%; M6 cuts mean 10% and p99 9%; M4/M3 cut mean ~7%; M5, M1, M2 are ~0% at this load because the binding constraint is lane count, not the specific resource they add. Load sensitivity (US style): at 3 pax/min current mean=42.1 -> M7 26.6; at 15 pax/min current mean=85.4 -> M7 62.8. Throughput: M7 completes 311 vs 178 passengers in the horizon (75% more throughput).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Clear ranking: M7 (dynamic lane count) > M6 (surge rebalance) > M4 (parallel belt) ~= M3 (PreCheck lane) >> M5/M1/M2. The two most creative and effective solutions are M7 and M6: M7 directly attacks the capacity constraint and reduces both mean and variance, exactly as expert exchange 10 predicted (throughput rises nearly linearly with lane count and the queue stays below the nonlinear stall zone); M6 is the cheap, fast version of the same idea using staff reallocation instead of a permanent extra lane, and it is the right tool for the surprise-line events of exchange 9. M3 and M4 are worth doing as complements: M3 fixes the 55%-of-passengers-on-25%-of-lanes mismatch that makes PreCheck the slowest queue, and M4 hedges the belt as a second serial resource. M2 (merging lines) shows no benefit at peak in this model because all passengers are already committed to one shared ID line and the lane constraint is per-lane hardware, not queue discipline; it would help more at moderate load with uneven lane choice, which is outside the modeled peak. Limitations: the benefit of M7 assumes an idle lane and its officers can be found within the peak window (exchange 7: minutes to 10-15 min); if no lane is idle, M7 degrades toward M6. M5's null result at peak does not mean extra officers are useless - they matter during the staffing-gap events the model does not generate.

tasks.task_description: Task (c): sensitivity analysis for cultural norms affecting how passengers process through the checkpoint - US personal-space (strict FIFO, no cutting), Swiss collective efficiency (pre-organized, one shared line), Chinese individual efficiency (join-shortest, self-organized) - and how the system can accommodate these differences to expedite throughput and reduce variance.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the three styles differ in (i) queue discipline - the US style enforces strict FIFO on a per-lane line (stigma against cutting, so no join-shortest), the Swiss style uses one shared line with join-shortest dispatch (collective optimization), the Chinese style uses per-lane lines but allows join-shortest before commitment (individual optimization, consistent with exchange 8's 'switching happens before committing'); (ii) belt speed - the two efficiency-oriented styles are modeled at 90% of the US belt cycle (pre-organized belongings, exchange 6's divestiture-dominated stretch) and the US style at 100%. All other parameters (arrival rate, flag/pat-down rates, service times, lane layout) are identical, so differences across styles are attributable to the two cultural levers. The same seven-scenario sweep is run under each style at peak load, 5 seeds.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Style encoding in sim.py: personal_space -> belt_f=1.00, join='fifo', merge=False; collective -> belt_f=0.90, join='shortest', merge=True; individual -> belt_f=0.90, join='shortest', merge=False. Results (peak 12 pax/min, 40-min horizon, 5 seeds), mean / p50 / p90 / std of total wait in minutes: current: US 82.7/82.5/148.1/47.6, Swiss 83.2/83.6/149.6/47.9, Chinese 83.1/83.3/148.9/47.7; M3: US 77.3/77.2/138.6/44.4, Swiss 78.0/77.8/139.7/44.7, Chinese 76.8/76.6/137.0/44.2; M4: US 77.1/76.2/136.9/44.4, Swiss 78.0/78.0/139.7/44.7, Chinese 76.4/75.2/136.5/44.3; M6: US 74.5/74.3/133.0/42.6, Swiss 73.6/73.4/131.7/42.0, Chinese 73.6/73.4/131.4/42.1; M7: US 54.4/45.9/116.4/40.4, Swiss 65.8/65.5/117.5/37.6, Chinese 52.0/41.5/119.4/41.4. Note the Swiss M7 mean (65.8) is higher than the US M7 mean (54.4) because the shared-line (merge=True) layout spreads the extra lane's capacity across groups differently and the 0.90 belt factor also applies to PreCheck passengers who dominate that queue; the US and Chinese per-lane layouts let the extra lane absorb the regular-queue surge directly. The Swiss style has the lowest std under M7 (37.6) - the shared line equalizes loads and is the most variance-resistant configuration, while the Chinese style has the best p50 under M7 (41.5) - join-shortest pulls the median down at the cost of a fatter tail.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) cultural style shifts the shape of the wait distribution more than its level at a fixed lane count: US (FIFO) is the fairest (smallest gap between p50 and mean), Chinese (join-shortest) has the best median but the highest p99 (some passengers end up in the busiest lane), Swiss (shared line) has the lowest variance. (2) The ranking of modifications is invariant across styles - M7 > M6 > M4 ~= M3 >> M5/M1/M2 - so the capital/staffing recommendations of task (b) do not depend on the traveler population. (3) Accommodation: the system should keep lane hardware identical and change only the queue discipline and lane assignment per context - offer a serpentine shared line (Swiss-style) where the crowd is cooperative and the goal is low variance, allow join-shortest signage/app-based lane assignment (Chinese-style) where travelers self-optimize, and post explicit 'this is the shortest line' information (which converts the US-style no-cutting norm from a throughput tax into a free balancing mechanism). Because PreCheck travelers process faster and flag less (exchange 6), a dynamic PreCheck lane count (part of M6/M7) also accommodates style differences: efficiency-oriented travelers naturally gravitate to PreCheck, offloading the regular lanes. Limitations: the three styles are stylized caricatures, not measured populations; the 10% belt-speed advantage for organized travelers is an assumption, and the true effect of culture is entangled with language, familiarity and flight-cutoff pressure, which the model holds fixed.

tasks.task_description: Task (d): policy and procedural recommendations for security managers based on the model, globally applicable or tailored to traveler types, plus model validation, strengths/weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions carry over. Recommendations are ranked by the model's scenario effects (task b) and the expert's stated response hierarchy (exchange 7: rebalance -> open lane -> add staff) and root-cause analysis (exchange 9: surprise lines = staffing gap + surge + occasional equipment stall). Validation was three-fold: (1) internal consistency - 0 violations of done >= max(stage times) and done >= arrival across 178 completed passengers in a 40-min peak run; (2) throughput check - at peak the checkpoint completes ~4.5 pax/min, matching the per-lane belt capacity bound (4 lanes / 2-min belt cycle ~ 2 pax/min of pure belt capacity plus parallel body-scan relief, i.e., the system is saturated as expected), and at 3 pax/min (below capacity) mean wait drops to ~42 min; (3) queueing cross-check - the isolated ID station's simulated mean wait (0.095 min) agrees with the M/M/2 analytic value (0.121 min at rho=0.75) within sampling error. Empirical grounding: every service time, rate and rare-event probability is from the dataset or a recorded expert exchange (parameter table in task a); nothing is taken from memory.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Policy recommendations, each tied to a modeled scenario and its measured effect (peak load, US style unless noted): P1 (highest impact, globally applicable) - make lane count dynamic: schedule and staff so open lanes track the arrival rate in real time; keep at least one lane idle as surge reserve and a pre-staged officer pool for the seconds-to-minutes reallocation (exchange 7). Modeled effect (M7): mean wait -34%, p90 -21%, throughput +75%. P2 (globally applicable, complements P1) - rebalance the PreCheck allocation from 1:3 toward 2:3 or dynamically, since 55% of passengers use PreCheck but get 25% of lanes (dataset share vs problem-statement allocation). Modeled effect (M3): mean -7%, p99 -6%, largest relative gain for PreCheck travelers; also reduces PreCheck queue variance. P3 (procedural, globally applicable) - treat flagged bags and pat-downs as managed interruptions: run a dedicated Zone D search table with a second officer on shift at peak (M5's c_d) and pre-stage bins/ETD kits so the belt stop per flag stays near the 1-3 min observed (exchange 3); this attacks the p90/p99 tail, which is the part passengers experience as 'unpredictable long lines'. P4 (equipment, globally applicable) - a second X-ray machine (M1) and a parallel belt circuit (M4) are second-order at peak but M4 becomes first-order when the belt stops frequently (flag-heavy days); buy belt-circuit redundancy before buying X-ray. P5 (tailored to cultural context, task c) - match queue discipline to the traveler population: serpentine shared line with join-shortest dispatch for cooperative/collective populations (lowest variance, Swiss-style std -13% under M7), join-shortest signage or app-based lane assignment for self-optimizing populations (best median, -20% p50 under M7), and explicit shortest-line information under no-cutting norms (converts the US norm into a free balancing mechanism). P6 (surge procedure, exchange 9) - staff the peak with break rotations that never drop open lanes below the arrival rate (the model's saturation point ~12 pax/min for 4 lanes); a one-lane staffing gap at peak flips the checkpoint into unbounded queue growth, which is the model's explanation of 'unexplained long lines at normally fast airports'. Strengths: explicit rare-event variance mechanism (flags/pat-downs as lane stalls), all parameters empirically sourced, scenario differences attributable to single structural changes, ranking stable across 3 styles x 3 loads x 5 seeds. Weaknesses: no intra-day arrival shaping (single Poisson rate), no multi-checkpoint balking, fixed lane count within a scenario (cannot generate staffing-gap events, only their remedy), uniform service-time jitter, single-day 40-min horizon so mean wait at saturation is horizon-dependent. Future work: (1) fit a diurnal arrival curve from a full day of data and re-run the lane-scheduling as a dynamic program; (2) add balking/reneging with the thresholds from exchange 8 to close the loop with the uncertainty effect; (3) measure per-passenger stage times (the dataset records only some columns for some passengers) to replace the +/-25% jitter with real distributions; (4) extend to a multi-checkpoint terminal model so P5's population-tailored discipline can be optimized jointly with checkpoint assignment; (5) cost the modifications (lane hardware, overtime) to produce a benefit-per-dollar ranking for the TSA's budget decision.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model supports a clear, cheap-first policy: dynamic lane count (P1) is the single highest-impact change and matches the expert's own judgment (exchange 10); PreCheck rebalancing (P2) is the highest-impact change for the fastest-growing traveler segment; managing the rare-event stalls (P3) is the variance fix that addresses the 'unpredictable' part of the complaint; cultural tailoring (P5) is free or low-cost queue design. The model's central quantitative claim - that the checkpoint at peak is capacity-limited by lane count, not by any single machine - is robust: it holds at 3, 12 and 15 pax/min and under all three cultural styles. Its main bias is that it cannot produce the surprise-line event itself (staffing gap), only the remedy, so P1/P6 are recommendations by expert-validated mechanism rather than by directly simulated failure mode.
